extracted.intended_audience: regulated entities, legal practitioners, policymakers, stakeholders, and public commenters concerned with EPA CAA section 202(a) findings and greenhouse gas regulation
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and scientific criteria EPA used to determine that emissions of certain greenhouse gases endanger public health and welfare and that emissions from new motor vehicles and engines cause or contribute to that air pollution under Clean Air Act section 202(a). Covers definition of the air pollutant, evidence standards, public health/welfare impact categories, contribution analysis, and procedural considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the 'air pollutant' as the aggregate group of six well-mixed greenhouse gases
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrator is defining the “air pollution” referred to in CAA section 202(a) to be the mix of six long-lived and directly-emitted greenhouse gases: carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), perfluorocarbons (PFCs), and sulfur hexafluoride (SF6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition is based on shared attributes: sufficiently long-lived to be well mixed globally, directly emitted, exert climate warming by trapping infrared heat, and are the focus of climate science and policy. Rationale and more precise meanings of “long lived” and “well mixed” provided in Section IV.A. The Administrator chose the aggregate group rather than treating each gas individually for the finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endangerment standard — 'reasonably anticipated to endanger public health and welfare'
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory threshold for an endangerment finding is whether greenhouse gases in the atmosphere may reasonably be anticipated both to endanger public health and to endanger public welfare under CAA section 202(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrator used judgment based on existing science, considering both observed and projected effects, and weighing identifiable risks and potential benefits. The statute's language is interpreted as precautionary and preventive; EPA does not need to find that subsequent control measures would prevent a substantial part of the danger, nor to find 'significant risk' as a minimum statutory requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence base and weight of scientific assessments
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings are based on careful consideration of the full weight of scientific evidence and a thorough review of major assessments (USGCRP, IPCC, NRC) and EPA's Technical Support Document (TSD).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA relies on major assessment reports and the TSD; uses observed and projected effects; applies IPCC/USGCRP terminology for likelihood and confidence. EPA places weight on areas with clear and strong evidence (e.g., water resources, sea level rise, adverse air quality impacts) and acknowledges uncertainties where present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public health impact criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Public health impacts considered include direct temperature effects, air quality effects (e.g., increased ambient ozone), effects on extreme weather events, effects on climate-sensitive diseases and aeroallergens, and related morbidity and mortality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA evaluated increases in ozone and heat-related mortality and morbidity, balancing uncertainties such as reductions in cold-related mortality. Evidence on extreme weather and coastal storm severity supports health endangerment. Vulnerable groups (children, elderly, poor) are given weight. Some areas (pathogen vectors, aeroallergens) provide directional support but with acknowledged uncertainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public welfare impact criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Public welfare impacts considered across sectors: food production and agriculture, forestry, water resources, sea level rise and coastal areas, energy/infrastructure and settlements, and ecosystems and wildlife.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA assessed present and future risks for each sector; water resources and sea level rise/coastal impacts provide the clearest and strongest support. Consideration includes extreme-event risks (wildfires, floods, drought), infrastructure vulnerabilities, ecosystem shifts, and potential near-term benefits for some crops offset by broader risks over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic scope of impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: The assessment focused on public health and public welfare impacts within the United States but also examined impacts in other world regions insofar as they can affect the U.S. population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA considers domestic impacts primarily but recognizes interdependence and that foreign impacts (e.g., migration, conflicts, supply disruptions) can affect U.S. welfare and strengthen the case for endangerment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal scope of impacts and accumulation
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA evaluated both current and projected (future) impacts, recognizing that risks and severity of adverse impacts are expected to increase over time with accumulating greenhouse gas concentrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA uses projected scenarios and places weight on foreseeable future conditions. For emissions accounting and comparability, GWPs with a 100-year time horizon are used (per UNFCCC/IPCC conventions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Global Warming Potential (GWP) 100-year CO2-equivalent units
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-lived greenhouse gases are compared and summed together on a CO2-equivalent basis by multiplying each gas by its GWP, using 100-year time frame values (per IPCC Second Assessment Report) and measuring in teragrams of CO2-equivalent (Tg CO2 eq).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the basis for aggregating different greenhouse gases for emissions comparisons (global and domestic) and for defining the aggregate air pollutant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause or contribute analysis methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether emissions from CAA section 202(a) source categories 'cause or contribute' to the air pollution that endangers public health and welfare, the Administrator compared emissions from those source categories to total global and total U.S. greenhouse gas emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA found section 202(a) sources account for ~4% of global and just over 23% of U.S. well-mixed GHG emissions. The analysis need not show 'significant' contribution or a bright-line threshold; global characteristics of climate change are an appropriate consideration. EPA reasonably relied on existing emissions (not required to project future new categories) and compared to both global and domestic totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement to find 'significant contribution' or bright line for contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrator does not need to find significant contribution, or establish a bright line, to conclude that a source category contributes to the air pollution that endangers public health and welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's reasoning: given the global nature of well-mixed GHGs and meaningful magnitude of emissions from section 202(a) sources, comparisons showing meaningful contributions suffice. The Supreme Court's Massachusetts v. EPA supports that motor-vehicle emissions make a meaningful contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of emissions data sources and comparison years
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrator used authoritative emissions data sources (e.g., WRI CAIT for global comparisons, EPA Inventory for U.S. data) and chose the most recent comprehensive years available for comparability (e.g., 2005 global, 2007 U.S. inventory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA updated U.S. emissions data since the Proposed Findings; notes methodological choices (e.g., year selection) and documents details in the TSD and docket.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration and exclusion of other climate forcers
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA explained why certain climate forcers (e.g., black carbon and other short-lived forcers) were not included in the defined air pollution for this finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA discussed ranges and uncertainties in climate forcing for such substances and gave rationale for excluding them from the aggregate 'well-mixed greenhouse gases' definition while explaining how they are treated in the science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory interpretation principles — precautionary/preventive approach
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrator interpreted the statutory language in section 202(a) as precautionary and preventive, meaning EPA may act based on reasonable anticipation of endangerment without requiring conclusive proof or a showing that controls will prevent the danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA summarized responses to legal comments: it does not need to find that control measures would prevent a substantial part of the danger, nor to demonstrate a high degree of quantified risk. This interpretation aligns with the cumulative and protective purposes of the statute and relevant case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public involvement and procedural adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule documents public involvement history (EPA's initial work, public comments since the proposed finding) and addresses issues raised regarding the rulemaking process (timeliness, separation from other rulemakings, adequacy of notice and comment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA concludes the notice-and-comment period was adequate and explains judicial review constraints: under CAA §307(b)(1) petitions for review must be filed in D.C. Circuit by a specified date, and under §307(d)(7)(B) only objections raised with reasonable specificity during the comment period may be raised in judicial review unless impracticable to raise earlier and central to outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of CAA section 202(a) source categories (transportation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 202(a) source categories covered include passenger cars, light- and heavy-duty trucks, buses, and motorcycles; transportation sources emit CO2, CH4, N2O, and HFCs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA quantifies that these transportation sources are responsible for ~23% of total annual U.S. greenhouse gas emissions and explained which emissions are included (e.g., hydrofluorocarbon emissions related to passenger compartment cooling are included; refrigeration units on trucks considered nonroad engines). Detailed emissions data is in Appendix B of EPA's TSD.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of adaptation, mitigation, and potential future regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA considered adaptation and mitigation, geographic and temporal scope, and impacts of potential future regulations and processes that generate greenhouse gas emissions in its evaluative approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although considered, adaptation/mitigation and implementation impacts do not negate the endangerment finding; EPA notes prior positions about whether an endangerment finding automatically makes GHGs 'subject to regulation' under other CAA programs and explains ongoing rulemakings (e.g., PSD tailoring rule) addressing such implementation issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting uncertainties and differential confidence across evidence types
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA acknowledged varying ability to characterize, quantify, and project risks and impacts, and used judgment to weigh threats for identifiable risks, placing greater weight on areas with clearer evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA explicitly notes uncertainties (e.g., in net health impacts from temperature changes, in pathogen/vector evidence) and states it will weigh potential benefits where relevant; it uses IPCC/USGCRP confidence/likelihood terminology to convey strength of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with prior EPA practice and Supreme Court precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA framed the finding as consistent with past EPA practice where appropriate and responsive to Massachusetts v. EPA, which recognized greenhouse gases can be 'air pollutants' under the CAA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA references legal precedent to justify defining the air pollutant and to support the conclusion that motor-vehicle emissions make a meaningful contribution; where prior EPA positions differ (e.g., PSD applicability), EPA explains current posture and related ongoing actions.
